p: After `first = EquipmentItem("E001", "Laptop", "Computer")`, which statement is correct?
c: first is an instance of EquipmentItem
why: Calling a class constructs an object; `first` refers to that instance.

p:
What is printed?

first = EquipmentItem("E1", "Laptop", "Computer")
second = EquipmentItem("E2", "Camera", "Media")
first.borrower_id = "M1"
print(second.borrower_id)
why: Instance attributes are independent; only `first` changed.

p: Which expression calls behaviour rather than reading stored state?
why: Parentheses call the method; the others read attributes.

p: What is the main role of `__init__` in this chapter?
why: The constructor establishes the state of each new instance.

p: Two separately constructed items have the same `item_id`. Which result is expected before custom equality is defined?
c: both names must refer to one object
Python rejects the second construction automatically
why: Equal-looking attributes do not make separately constructed objects identical.

p: Which situation most strongly justifies introducing a class?
c: several operations must preserve one entity's changing state
why: Classes earn their cost when related state and rules need one boundary.

p: A method is defined as `def label(): ...` inside a class and called with `item.label()`. What is missing?
why: An ordinary instance method receives the object as its first parameter.

c: ask first to perform loan_to using M014
why: The receiver is named on the left; the argument supplies request data.

p: When may dictionaries and functions remain clearer than a class?
c: when records are few, passive, and have little related behaviour
why: The course treats classes as a design choice, not an automatic replacement.
